name: Ezekiel
v: In the seventh year, on the tenth day of the fifth month, some of Israel's elders came to inquire of the LORD. They sat down in front of me.
The word of the LORD hit me:
"Son of man, speak to Israel's elders. Tell them: This is what the Sovereign LORD says — Have you come to consult me? As I live, I will not be consulted by you. Declaration of the Sovereign LORD.
Will you judge them, son of man? Will you judge them? Then confront them with the atrocities of their ancestors.

Tell them: This is what the Sovereign LORD says — On the day I chose Israel, I raised my hand in oath to the offspring of Jacob's house. I revealed myself to them in Egypt. I raised my hand and swore: I am the LORD your God.
That same day I swore I would bring them out of Egypt into a land I had scouted for them — flowing with milk and honey, the jewel of every land.
I told them: Each of you, throw away the obscenities you've been staring at. Don't defile yourselves with the gutter-gods of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.

But they rebelled. They refused to listen. Not one of them threw away the obscenities they were staring at. None abandoned the gutter-gods of Egypt. So I said I would pour out my fury on them, spend my anger on them right there in the land of Egypt.
But I acted for the sake of my name — so it wouldn't be dragged through the mud in front of the nations they lived among, the nations who had watched me reveal myself to bring Israel out of Egypt.
So I brought them out of Egypt and led them into the wilderness.
I gave them my statutes. I made my judgments known to them — the path by which a person lives, if they live by it.
I also gave them my Sabbaths as a sign between us, so they would know that I, the LORD, am the One who sets them apart.

But Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness. They didn't walk in my statutes. They threw away my judgments — the very path by which a person lives. They desecrated my Sabbaths, again and again. So I said I would pour out my fury on them in the wilderness and finish them.
But I acted for the sake of my name — so it wouldn't be dragged through the mud in front of the nations who had watched me bring them out.
Still, I raised my hand in the wilderness and swore I would not bring them into the land I had given them — flowing with milk and honey, the jewel of every land —
because they had thrown away my judgments, refused to walk in my statutes, and desecrated my Sabbaths. Their hearts kept chasing their gutter-gods.
Yet I looked on them with pity. I didn't destroy them. I didn't wipe them out in the wilderness.
In the wilderness I said to their children: Don't walk in the ways of your parents. Don't keep their rulings. Don't defile yourselves with their gutter-gods.
I am the LORD your God. Walk in my statutes. Keep my judgments. Live them.
Set apart my Sabbaths. Let them be a sign between us, so you'll know I am the LORD your God.

But the children rebelled too. They didn't walk in my statutes. They didn't keep my judgments — didn't live them, the very path by which a person lives. They desecrated my Sabbaths. So I said I would pour out my fury on them, spend my anger on them in the wilderness.
But I held back my hand. I acted for the sake of my name — so it wouldn't be dragged through the mud in front of the nations who had watched me bring them out.
Still, I raised my hand in the wilderness and swore I would scatter them among the nations, fling them across the lands —
because they hadn't kept my judgments, had thrown away my statutes, had desecrated my Sabbaths, and their eyes were locked on the gutter-gods of their ancestors.
So I gave them over to statutes that weren't good and judgments by which they could not live.
I let them defile themselves with their own gifts — letting them pass every firstborn through the fire — so I could devastate them, so they would know I am the LORD.
So speak to the house of Israel, son of man. Tell them: This is what the Sovereign LORD says — Even in this your ancestors blasphemed me by their treachery against me.

When I brought them into the land I had sworn to give them, they looked around at every high hill, every leafy tree, and there they offered their sacrifices, presented their provocations, sent up their pleasing aromas, poured out their drink offerings.
I asked them: What's this high place you keep running to? They still call it Bamah — the high place — to this day.
So tell the house of Israel: This is what the Sovereign LORD says — Are you defiling yourselves the way your ancestors did? Whoring after their obscenities?

When you lift up your gifts, when you pass your children through the fire, you are still defiling yourselves with every gutter-god of yours — to this day. And you expect me to be consulted by you, house of Israel? As I live, declaration of the Sovereign LORD, I will not be consulted by you.
What you imagine will never happen. You keep saying, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the lands — serving wood and stone.'
As I live, declaration of the Sovereign LORD, I will rule over you with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and fury poured out.
I will bring you out from the peoples. I will gather you from the lands where you've been scattered — with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and fury poured out.
I will bring you into the wilderness of the peoples. And there, face to face, I will enter judgment with you.
Just as I entered judgment with your ancestors in the wilderness of Egypt, so I will enter judgment with you. Declaration of the Sovereign LORD.
I will make you pass under the shepherd's rod. I will bring you into the bond of the covenant.

I will purge from you the rebels — the ones who have broken faith with me. I will bring them out of the land where they're staying, but they will not enter the land of Israel. Then you will know I am the LORD.

As for you, house of Israel — this is what the Sovereign LORD says — Go on, then. Each of you, serve your gutter-gods. But after this — you will listen to me. And you will no longer profane my holy name with your gifts and your idols.

For on my holy mountain — the high mountain of Israel, declaration of the Sovereign LORD — there the whole house of Israel, all of them, will serve me in the land. There I will accept them. There I will require your contributions, the firstfruits of your offerings, all your holy gifts.
I will accept you as a pleasing aroma when I bring you out from the peoples and gather you from the lands where you've been scattered. Through you I will show myself holy in the eyes of the nations.
Then you will know I am the LORD — when I bring you into the land of Israel, the land I raised my hand and swore to give your ancestors.
There you will remember your ways, every deed by which you defiled yourselves. You will loathe yourselves to your face for all the evils you committed.

And you will know I am the LORD when I deal with you for the sake of my name — not according to your evil ways, not according to your corrupt deeds, house of Israel. Declaration of the Sovereign LORD.
The word of the LORD hit me:
"Son of man, set your face toward the south. Preach against the south. Prophesy against the forest of the Negev.

Tell the forest of the Negev: Hear the word of the LORD. This is what the Sovereign LORD says — I am about to kindle a fire in you. It will devour every green tree in you and every dry tree. The blazing flame will not be put out. Every face from south to north will be scorched by it.
Every living thing will see that I, the LORD, kindled it. It will not be put out."
Then I said, "Sovereign LORD, they're saying about me, 'Isn't he just spinning riddles?'"

com.d:
# A God Who Remembers His Covenant

The spiritual heart of Ezekiel 20 is God's steadfast commitment to His people despite their repeated rebellion—He chooses to preserve them for the sake of His own name and covenant promise, not because they deserve it.

When the elders of Israel come seeking God's word, the Lord instructs Ezekiel to confront them with their history of unfaithfulness. From Egypt to the wilderness and beyond, Israel had constantly turned from God's statutes, ignored His sabbaths, and worshiped idols. Yet at every stage where judgment seemed certain and justified, God withheld His full wrath. He did not destroy them in the wilderness as He might have. Why? Because God's reputation was at stake. To destroy His redeemed people would suggest His power was hollow or His promises were empty. God's self-respect, so to speak, became their salvation.

This speaks to something profound about grace. We often imagine mercy as God overlooking our sin because He feels sorry for us. But Ezekiel reveals something deeper: God's covenant love is bound up with His own character and honor. When God makes a promise, He stakes His integrity on it. Our salvation does not ultimately rest on our worthiness—we could never be worthy—but on God's unwavering commitment to His word.

This truth transforms how we view both judgment and forgiveness in our own lives. When we stumble, when we cycle through seasons of faithfulness and failure, we are not simply at God's whim. We are held by His covenant oath. God does not save us because we finally got our act together. He saves us because He has bound Himself to us through Christ, and His honor demands He be faithful even when we are faithless.

What covenant promises of God are you tempted to doubt? How might trusting that God's honor is invested in keeping His word reshape your confidence in Him today?
com.s:
Ezekiel 20 presents one of the most theologically dense historical retrospectives in prophetic literature, delivered in the eleventh year of Jehoiachin's exile (591 BCE) when elders of Israel approach the prophet seeking an oracle from YHWH. The chapter functions as a sustained covenant lawsuit (*rîb*) that systematically recounts Israel's history of rebellion from Egypt through the wilderness to Canaan, uniquely emphasizing that apostasy characterized the nation from its very inception rather than representing later decline from an idealized past.

The passage opens with YHWH's startling refusal to be consulted (*dārash*), a term denoting formal prophetic inquiry, immediately establishing the tension between Israel's religious pretensions and their actual covenant fidelity. The divine response transforms their request into an occasion for judgment, with the repeated rhetorical question "Will you judge them?" inviting Ezekiel to prosecute the case. Throughout the historical recital, the phrase "for my name's sake" (*lemaʿan shemî*) appears as a theological leitmotif, revealing that Israel's preservation stemmed not from their merit but from YHWH's concern for his reputation among the nations—a striking qualification of election theology.

The chapter's most controversial element appears in verses 25-26, where YHWH declares he gave Israel "statutes that were not good" and "ordinances by which they could not live," specifically referencing child sacrifice. Interpretive approaches vary considerably: some scholars read this as divine accommodation to Israel's hardened condition, others as ironic reference to pagan laws Israel adopted, and still others as describing YHWH's permissive will allowing consequences of their choices. This passage has generated substantial debate regarding divine agency and moral responsibility in prophetic theology.

The conclusion shifts dramatically toward restoration hope, envisioning a new exodus where YHWH will purge rebels in the "wilderness of the peoples" before bringing a refined remnant to the holy mountain. This eschatological reframing transforms the judgment oracle into covenant renewal, with worship restored "on my holy mountain, the mountain height of Israel." The canonical placement alongside chapters 16 and 23 creates a triptych of historical allegories interpreting Israel's persistent unfaithfulness, while anticipating the restoration oracles of chapters 34-37.
com.p:
Ezekiel chapter twenty stands as a devastating prophetic indictment delivered approximately 591 years before the birth of Christ, during the Babylonian exile when the elders of Israel came to inquire of the Lord through His prophet. This chapter occupies a pivotal position in redemptive history—after the fall of Jerusalem's first siege, during the exile judgment, yet before the final destruction of the temple in 586 BC. Within the grand arc of Scripture, this passage sits squarely in the period of covenant judgment, when God was purging His people through the fires of Babylonian captivity as discipline for centuries of accumulated rebellion.

The Lord refuses to be inquired of by these elders, instead commanding Ezekiel to confront them with the abominations of their fathers. What follows is a sweeping historical recitation unlike any other in Scripture—a prophetic rehearsal of Israel's rebellion traced through four generations: Egypt, the wilderness, the second wilderness generation, and the land of Canaan. In each epoch, God reveals His gracious initiative followed by Israel's stubborn idolatry, then His restraint of full judgment "for the sake of My name." This refrain echoes throughout the chapter, establishing that God's redemptive purposes ultimately rest not on human faithfulness but on His own covenant commitment and glory.

The typological weight of this passage is immense. Israel's repeated cycle of rebellion in the wilderness shadows humanity's universal condition—given grace upon grace yet turning perpetually to idols. The "statutes that were not good" permitted to the rebellious generation typologically anticipates Paul's teaching that the law, though holy, became an instrument of death to those under sin's dominion. Yet even here, the promise of a second exodus emerges with stunning clarity: God declares He will bring Israel into "the wilderness of the peoples" and there plead with them face to face, purging out the rebels while bringing the remnant into covenant bond.

This prophecy finds its initial fulfillment in the post-exilic restoration, its deeper realization in Christ's gathering of a remnant through the gospel, and its ultimate consummation when all Israel shall be saved at the Lord's return. The "high mountain of Israel" where acceptable worship will finally occur points forward to the heavenly Zion, the true Jerusalem above.

For the church living between the advents, this chapter stands as both warning and comfort—warning that religious externalism without heart transformation brings judgment, yet comfort that God's purposes cannot fail. His name will be sanctified among the nations through a faithful remnant, purified and gathered by sovereign grace alone.
